# Efficient Ground-State Manifold Amplification for Rydberg Atom Arrays via Houdayer Cluster Updates

We demonstrate a hybrid quantum-classical approach for exploring ground-state manifolds of maximum independent set problems, in which quantum hardware supplies the initial solutions and an entirely classical post-processing algorithm expands them, increasing the solution diversity of quantum hardware measurements by several orders of magnitude. Quantum optimization devices, while capable of generating high-quality solutions, can suffer from fundamental sampling limitations. This is particularly problematic for applications that strongly depend on a large variety of uncorrelated optimal solutions. We apply the Houdayer cluster update algorithm to systematically expand quantum-generated solution sets through classical post-processing. We validate our approach on a test bed of 43 problem instances from QuEra’s Aquila analog annealing device, achieving diversity amplification factors, defined as the increase in the number of distinct solutions at a given set size, of up to \(11923\times\) with a median of \(24.3\times\) across different problem scales and hardness parameters. Because exact ground-state degeneracies are known for these instances, the recovered fraction of the manifold can be measured rather than bounded: post-processing recovers a median of 21% of the ground-state manifold, and provably all of it for six instances. We also demonstrate that, in some cases, the classical post-processing can discover independent sets larger than those found by the quantum hardware, thus improving on solution quality and not just diversity. While the method is non-ergodic and cannot guarantee complete manifold coverage, it consistently discovers a larger number of high-quality, and in some cases strictly better, configurations than quantum sampling alone. This work demonstrates how simple classical post-processing can enhance the utility of quantum optimization results.

### I. INTRODUCTION

The maximum independent set (MIS) problem is a paradigmatic NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem [1], which remains NP-hard on unit disk graphs [2], with applications spanning network design, computational biology, and portfolio optimization. Given an undirected graph _G_=(_V,E_), the goal is to find the largest subset \(S\subseteq V\) such that no two vertices in _S_ are adjacent. Neutral atom arrays with programmable geometries have emerged as a leading platform for quantum optimization of MIS problems [3-5]. In these systems, atoms are positioned with sub-micrometer precision and coupled via Rydberg blockade interactions that naturally encode the MIS problem on unit disk graphs, as originally proposed in Ref. [3]. The blockade radius _r<sub>b</sub>_ defines the graph connectivity: edges connect atoms within distance _r<sub>b</sub>_, while independence constraints arise from the strong energetic suppression, rather than strict impossibility, of simultaneous Rydberg excitation within the blockade sphere. Recent experiments on Rydberg atom arrays [4], including QuEra’s Aquila quantum device [6, 7], have demonstrated quantum annealing algorithms (QAA) capable of generating high-quality solutions of MIS problems with hundreds of atoms.

However, quantum optimization devices face a fundamental sampling limitation. While capable of accessing

optimal or near-optimal configurations, quantum measurements from a typical hardware run produce only tens to hundreds of distinct (degenerate) solutions (for example, ranging from 2 to 493 in the data set of Ref. [7] studied here). Moreover, quantum annealers have been shown to be biased samplers, both on superconducting hardware [8, 9] and on Rydberg atom arrays [10]: they do not find all ground states with equal probability. This biased sampling becomes problematic when the ground- state manifold contains exponentially many degenerate optimal configurations as is often the case for the MIS. However, the classical post-processing presented in this work reveals that the aforementioned unit disk graph instances can have as many as 10<sup>3</sup> to 10<sup>6</sup> distinct maximum independent sets, with the largest manifold explored containing nearly 2 million optimal configurations. These counts are specific to instances of a few hundred atoms, and the degeneracy grows rapidly with size, so larger devices should make the sampling problem worse rather than better. The limited sampling diversity of quantum hardware leaves vast regions of these degenerate manifolds unexplored, restricting practical utility for applications requiring multiple diverse solutions such as ensemble methods and entropy calculations, design space exploration, post-optimization inclusion of constraints, or robustness analysis, to name a few.

Classical post-processing provides a mechanism to amplify quantum-generated solution diversity. In previous

<tbc>work [11], we introduced an algorithm based on Houdayer cluster updates [12] to improve sampling from biased optimizers. The approach operates through rejection-free cluster exchanges at zero temperature: given two independent sets {_s<sub>i</sub>_} and {_s<sub>j</sub>_}, the algorithm computes their symmetric difference \(\Delta_{ij}=s_i\oplus s_j\) (vertices present in exactly one solution), identifies the _c_ connected components (clusters) in the induced subgraph \(G[\Delta_{ij}]\), which we refer to as the disagreement graph, and generates 2_<sup>c</sup>_ candidate configurations by independently choosing which clusters to exchange. This mechanism preserves solution quality, and can occasionally improve it (Section IIID), while enabling large-scale structural rearrangements that can reach configurations unavailable to local moves.

While fundamentally non-ergodic, i.e., offering no guarantee of complete manifold coverage, the method proved effective at reducing sampling bias in quantum annealing data from D-Wave systems and improving diversity for classical spin-glass solvers [11], whose sampling biases are documented in Refs. [8, 9, 13, 14].

The present work applies this approach to MIS measurement records from Rydberg atom arrays. Applied to two independent sets, the cluster exchange keeps every candidate independent by construction (Section IIC), so none is rejected as infeasible. We use the method to ask how much ground-state information a neutral atom measurement record contains beyond the solutions the device reports. Because the instances studied here come with exact reference optima and exact ground-state degeneracies, we can measure both how many additional optimal configurations the record yields and what fraction of the true manifold that represents. We source initial solution pools from quantum hardware runs on QuEra’s Aquila quantum device, using quantum measurements as high-quality seeds for classical cluster-based exploration. Raw hardware measurements may select adjacent atoms, and these are repaired through a two-stage greedy procedure [7]. The first stage iteratively removes the vertices with most conflicts until independence is restored, and the second greedily adds vertices that maintain independence to recover maximality. This repair process runs in O(|_E_|) time per candidate and typically preserves optimal or near-optimal set sizes.

We evaluate our approach on 43 problem instances across three categories whose hardness parameter spans several orders of magnitude: Benchmark instances (137 atoms each), hard instances [7] that classical kernelization alone cannot reduce to an empty kernel (115 - 231 atoms), and standard instances (7 - 205 atoms). The quantum seeds come from measurements on QuEra’s Rydberg quantum device, with solution counts ranging from 2 to 493 distinct configurations per instance at the size the hardware reached. Our classical post-processing systematically processes quantum solution pairs through Houdayer cluster updates, applying adaptive stopping criteria to balance manifold exploration against computational cost.

The results demonstrate amplification across the full<tbc>

<tbc>dataset: solution diversity increases by factors ranging from \(1\times\) to \(11923\times\), with the quantum seed pool expanded to contain hundreds or thousands of distinct configurations at the seed size in seconds to minutes on commodity hardware [15]. Discovery dynamics reveal that manifold exploration proceeds efficiently until saturation, with most new solutions discovered within the first few hundred to few thousand pair proceedings. We develop stopping criteria based on discovery rate saturation (halt when the number of newly discovered solutions over a sliding window of 500 consecutive pairs falls below 0.1% of the current pool size) and computational budgets (10<sup>5</sup> pair limit), enabling practical termination without exhaustive enumeration.

For three instances (`L12\_seed829`, `L17\_seed424`, and `L17\_seed46`), the classical algorithm discovered independent sets _larger_ than those found by quantum hardware yielding solution quality improvements, not merely diversity amplification within a known manifold. These cases involve size increases from 35 to 36 atoms (`L12\_seed829`) and from 68 and 67 to 70 atoms (`L17` instances), demonstrating that classical post-processing can improve upon quantum optimization results for analog quantum optimizers that are inherently noisy. As we detail below, these improvements reach the exact optimum in one case and come within one atom of it in the other two.

This work makes the following contributions:

1. **How much a measurement record contains:** quantification, across 43 instances spanning three hardness families, of the additional distinct configurations recoverable from a neutral atom measurement record beyond those the device reports, a median of \(24.3\times\) overall and \(8.9\times\) over the 35 instances whose seeds were already optimal, reaching \(11923\times\) for `HP1478`, for 18 minutes of laptop time across the entire dataset, measured end to end.<tbc>

2. **Coverage measured against exact degeneracies:** because exact ground-state degeneracies are available for these instances, the recovered _fraction_ of the manifold is measured rather than bounded, a median of 21% and provably complete on six instances. This converts the non-ergodicity of the method from a disclaimer into a measured quantity, and shows that completeness is attainable precisely when the manifold is small enough for a fixed seed budget to enumerate.<tbc>

3. **An audit of what the hardware determined:** comparison against exact reference optima shows the quantum seed pool sat strictly below the true optimum on 8 of the 43 instances, including six of the nine hard instances. On three of these, classical recombination discovered strictly larger independent sets than the hardware found, reaching the exact optimum on one. Distinguishing an amplified true manifold from an amplified suboptimal one requires such a reference.

4. **Adaptive stopping criterion**: saturation-based termination that keeps the recovery cost negligible relative to the hardware run being post-processed, with a bounded worst case.<tbc>

5. **Application of cluster updates to Rydberg atom array MIS**: We apply the cluster updates previously developed for classical solvers and superconducting annealers on quadratic binary optimization problems without field terms \[11\], to independent sets sampled by neutral atom hardware, with a feasibility argument showing that the exchange respects the independence constraint by construction.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the instances studied, quantum hardware setup, Houdayer cluster update algorithm, MIS repair procedure, and the stopping criterion. Section III presents amplification results, classical improvements, discovery dynamics, and efficiency analysis. Section IV discusses implications, limitations, and connections to related work. Section V concludes with future directions.

## II. METHODS

Our approach follows the hybrid quantum-classical workflow illustrated in Figure 1. Quantum hardware runs on QuEra’s Aquila quantum device generate an initial pool of candidate solutions for each problem instance. These quantum-generated samples are then passed to a classical post-processing pipeline based on Houdayer cluster updates \[11, 12\], which systematically recombine solution pairs to discover further distinct configurations at the same set size. Whether that size is the true optimum depends on the seed pool and is established separately in Section II F. The expanded solution pool is validated and the amplification factor is recorded. Throughout, S<sub>0</sub> denotes the seed pool, the distinct repaired solutions at the largest size _k_ reached in the hardware record, and S<sub>final</sub> the solutions held at the final size \(k_\mathrm{final}\ge k\) once post-processing terminates. The amplification factor is their ratio, _A=N_<sub>total</sub>_/N_<sub>quantum</sub>=|S<sub>final</sub>|/|S<sub>0</sub>|, with _N_<sub>quantum</sub>=|S<sub>0</sub>| and _N_<sub>total</sub>=|S<sub>final</sub>|. For the three instances whose size improved, _A_ and all aggregate statistics use the first pass at the seed size, and their pools at the improved size are reported in Section III D. The following subsections describe each component of the pipeline.

### A. Problem Instances

We evaluate our approach on 43 problem instances sourced from quantum hardware runs on QuEra’s Aquila quantum device from the study in Ref. \[7\], spanning three categories that cover a wide range of problem sizes and hardness regimes.

The **Benchmark Competition** category comprises four site-diluted union-jack graph instances (`HP125`, `HP1412`, `HP1435`, and `HP1478`), each with 137 atoms on a square lattice of side length _L_=14 \[7\]. The instance labels are mnemonics for the hardness parameter _H_ of Ref. \[7\] rather than a literal digit-by-digit encoding of it (`HP1478`, `HP1412`, `HP125`, and `HP1435` denote _H_=1.478, 14.12, 125.5, and 1435, respectively). The hardness parameter is the classical, conductance-like degeneracy ratio _H=D_<sub>|MIS|-1</sub>/(|MIS|_D_<sub>|MIS|</sub>), where \(D_\alpha\) is the number of independent sets of size \(\alpha\) \[16\], and the QAA success probability is suppressed exponentially in _H_ \[7\]. These four values range from near-trivial to seemingly intractable for unassisted QAA. The reference data of Refs. \[7, 17\] record _D_<sub>|MIS|-1</sub> for the other 39 instances, so _H_ is available for all 43 and spans 1.03 to 9717.

The **Hard** category comprises nine instances (115 to 231 atoms) on which Ref. \[7\] ran its qReduMIS pipeline on hardware. Their seeds come from the full-graph QAA runs of the same reference, as for the other families (Section IIB). On these instances the classical reduction rules stall before the kernel is eliminated, leaving a residual subproblem that quantum hardware is used to unblock, making them among the most challenging optimization problems in the dataset.

The **Standard test bed** category comprises thirty _L_=3 - _L_=16 instances (\(n=L\times L\) lattice sites and with 7 - 205 atoms) from the QAA hardware test bed \[4, 7\]. These fully-reducible instances span a wide range of problem sizes and graph structures arising from the unit disk constraint. Full instance specifications and quantum measurement data for both categories are provided in Refs. \[7, 17\].

### B. Quantum Hardware and Solution Seeds

Each problem instance is encoded as a unit disk graph on QuEra’s Aquila quantum device, where atoms are positioned at graph vertices and the Rydberg blockade radius defines graph connectivity \[4, 6\]. The device executes a time-dependent Hamiltonian evolution governed by global Rabi frequency and detuning controls, with the problem structure encoded through the atomic positions together with the blockade radius, which is itself set by the laser parameters. Following Ref. \[7\], with \(\hbar=1\), the Hamiltonian is

\(\mathcal{H}(t)=\frac{\Omega(t)}{2}\sum_i\left(e^{\mathrm{i}\phi(t)}|0\rangle_i\langle 1|+\mathrm{h}.\mathrm{c}.\right)-\delta(t)\sum_in_i+\sum_{i<j}V_{ij}n_in_j,\text{(1)}\)

where \(|0\rangle_i\) and \(|1\rangle_i\) are the ground and Rydberg states of atom _i_, \(n_i=|1\rangle_i\langle 1|\) is its occupation operator, \(\Omega(t)\) and \(\phi(t)\) are the Rabi frequency and phase of the global drive, and \(\delta(t)\) is the laser detuning. The interaction

<tbc>_V<sub>ij</sub>=C_<sub>6</sub>/|**x**_<sub>i</sub>_-**x**_<sub>j</sub>_|<sup>6</sup> is the van der Waals coupling between atoms at positions **x**_<sub>i</sub>_ and **x**_<sub>j</sub>_, with _C_<sub>6</sub> the van der Waals coefficient. Unlike the zero-field spin glasses for which Houdayer cluster updates were developed \[12\], this Hamiltonian contains a field term, the detuning \(\delta(t)\) acting on every _n<sub>i</sub>_. At the conclusion of each quantum anneal, whose duration is of order microseconds, projective site-resolved measurements yield a classical bit string indicating the Rydberg state of each atom. Raw outcomes that violate independence constraints due to finite blockade strength or imperfect adiabaticity are repaired using the procedure described in Section IID. Repeating this process over many shots yields an initial pool S<sub>0</sub> of distinct solutions at the largest size the hardware attained, which Section IIF compares against the certified optimum.

All 43 seed pools derive from direct anneals on the full problem instance (1000 shots per instance \[7\], of which 49 to 946, median 426, survive post-selection for correct atom loading), and the repair step leaves most of each measurement intact: on average 92% to 94% of the atoms<tbc>

<tbc>in a repaired seed come from the measurement itself for the 30 standard instances, and 90% to 93% for the nine hard instances. For the hard family these are the vanilla QAA runs on the full graph that Ref. \[7\] reports as the baseline for its qReduMIS pipeline, not the kernel measurements taken inside that pipeline. The qReduMIS pipeline itself is considerably stronger and reaches the optimum on all nine instances.

Across our 43-instance dataset, the seed pools hold between 2 and 493 distinct solutions (mean 57.0, median 16). On six instances (`L12\_seed2922`, `L14\_seed1590`, `L14\_seed2358`, `L14\_seed2480`, `L15\_seed3591`, and `L17\_seed424`) only one solution reaches the best MIS size, and the implementation pairs it with the best solution one atom smaller, so their pools of two include that solution. On 35 of the 43 instances that size is the certified optimum (Section IIF). Eighteen instances yielded fewer than 10 unique solutions, 16 produced between 10 and 99, and 9 produced between 100 and 493. <tbc>which are known to exhibit biased sampling and do not find all ground-state configurations with equal probability for a given seed. This has been established both on superconducting annealing hardware \[8, 9\] and, for Rydberg atom arrays of the kind used here, in Ref. \[10\]. That Houdayer cluster updates improve precisely this class of sampling bias was established extensively for spin-glass optimizers in earlier work \[11\]. Here we apply the same principle to independent sets returned by quantum hardware, with the added requirement that the hard independence constraint of the MIS be respected throughout. It is this limited and non-uniform coverage that motivates classical post-processing.

## C. Houdayer Cluster Updates

The Houdayer cluster update algorithm \[12\] was originally developed for two-dimensional spin-glass systems and has since been extended to higher-dimensional binary systems in regimes (e.g., temperature or dimensionality) where clusters do not percolate \[18\] and thus are effective in resampling configurations of the system and improving thermalization when simulated via Monte Carlo methods. More recently, it has been applied to improve sampling from biased quantum and classical optimizers \[11\]. The core idea is to recombine pairs of solutions through non-local cluster exchanges, generating many new candidate configurations from a single pair in a rejection-free manner (i.e., not affecting the combined energy of the system).

Given two solution configurations _s<sub>i</sub>_ and _s<sub>j</sub>_, the algorithm first computes their symmetric difference \(\Delta_{ij}=s_i\oplus s_j\), i.e., the set of vertices on which the two solutions disagree. The agreement backbone \(s_i\cap s_j\) remains fixed throughout. The induced subgraph \(G[\Delta_{ij}]\) is then decomposed into _c_ connected components, each representing an independent region of disagreement. Because these components are disconnected in \(G[\Delta_{ij}]\), the vertex assignments within each cluster can be swapped independently without affecting any other cluster. Enumerating every binary exchange pattern, each specifying for each cluster whether to take vertices from _s<sub>i</sub>_ or _s<sub>j</sub>_, yields 2_<sup>c</sup>_ candidate solutions from a single pair. Every such candidate is independent by construction, because each cluster contributes vertices from one parent only, no edge of _G_ joins distinct components of \(G[\Delta_{ij}]\), and a backbone vertex cannot be adjacent to a selected vertex of either parent. When _s<sub>i</sub>_ and _s<sub>j</sub>_ have equal size, a further consequence follows. Complementary candidates, obtained by exchanging every cluster, have total size |_s<sub>i</sub>_|+|_s<sub>j</sub>_|, so if that common size is the maximum independent set size neither candidate can exceed it and both must equal it. Every cluster of two maximum independent sets is therefore balanced between the two parents, and the exchange is size-preserving without any rejection step. If instead the parents share a suboptimal size, individual clusters may be imbalanced, and taking the larger side of such a<tbc>

<tbc>cluster yields a strictly larger independent set. This is the mechanism behind the quality improvements of Section IIID: for `L12\_seed829`, 17 of the 2016 seed pairs contain at least one imbalanced cluster, and for `L17\_seed46` all 6 do, and each of those yields a valid solution at least one vertex larger than the seeds. For suboptimal parents a candidate can also be non-maximal, and the repair of Section IID then adds vertices. All 2_<sup>c</sup>_ patterns are enumerated without a cap on _c_, whose largest observed value was 14.

Starting from the initial quantum seed pool S<sub>0</sub> at the best-found size _k_, the algorithm iterates over the \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{|\mathcal{S}_0|}{2}\) pairs drawn from the seed pool, collecting newly discovered solutions of size _k_ into the output pool as they are found. Discovered solutions are not themselves re-paired: the pair list is fixed by S<sub>0</sub>, so the number of exchange operations is bounded a priori rather than growing with the pool, and within a pass every recovered configuration is a single recombination of two of its seeds. Solutions are stored as frozen sets of vertex indices for O(1) deduplication via hash lookup, so each configuration is counted only once regardless of how many pairs produce it. Candidates larger than _k_ are collected separately and, once the pass ends, the largest of them seed a new pass at that size, repeated until a pass finds nothing larger. These further passes are what enable classical post-processing to surpass the size of the seed pool on hard instances. The algorithm terminates with an expanded pool S<sub>final</sub> of optimum size \(k_\mathrm{final}\ge k\), and the amplification factor _A_=|S<sub>final</sub>|/|S<sub>0</sub>| is recorded.

## D. MIS Repair

Two operations in the pipeline can yield a set that is not a maximal independent set: raw hardware measurements, which may select adjacent atoms when the blockade is imperfect, and cluster exchange, which preserves independence (Section IIC) but can leave a vertex addable. We handle both with a two-stage greedy procedure adapted from Ref. \[7\]. Only its first stage is ever required for raw measurements, and only its second for exchange candidates. In the first stage, vertices are removed iteratively in order of decreasing conflict degree, the number of neighbors also in the current set, until no violations remain. This greedy ordering minimizes the number of removals needed to reach feasibility. In the second stage, vertices outside the current set are added greedily in order of increasing degree in the remaining graph, so that each addition leaves as many future candidates unblocked as possible. This extension continues until no further vertex can be added without creating a conflict, restoring maximality. The full procedure runs in O(|_E_|) time, with _E_ the number of edges of the graph, per candidate and in practice preserves the optimal set size for the large majority of repaired solutions. A small fraction of candidates repair to a smaller-than-optimal set and are discarded.

### E. Adaptive Stopping Criteria

Processing all \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{|S|}{2}\) pairs is feasible when the solution pool is small, but becomes prohibitively expensive as the pool grows during exploration. We therefore implement an adaptive stopping strategy that selects among three modes at runtime. When the total pair count is below 10<sup>4</sup>, the algorithm runs exhaustively, guaranteeing complete pairwise coverage. For larger pools, it monitors the discovery rate over a sliding window of 500 consecutive pairs and halts when the number of new solutions found within that window falls below 0.1% of the current pool size, indicating that the accessible manifold region has been saturated. A hard cutoff of 10<sup>5</sup> pairs bounds the number of pair comparisons regardless of discovery dynamics, although this limit was never reached in our experiments. The largest number of pairs processed in any single pass was 16539, and in any higher-level pass 6951 (the second-level pass of `L17\_seed46`).

### F. Validation

As a safeguard against implementation error, rather than as a test of the algorithm, all solutions in S<sub>final</sub> are validated post-hoc by verifying independence (no edge connects two selected vertices), maximality (no unselected vertex can be added without creating a conflict), and target cardinality (solution size equals _k_<sub>final</sub>). This last check confirms membership at the size the run reached, which coincides with the certified optimum only where the two agree. It is not an independent test of global optimality. The protocol was applied to all 15511 solutions from the three instances where classical post- processing discovered a larger independent set than the quantum hardware, with a 100% pass rate. Throughout, the reference (true) maximum independent set size of each instance is taken from the reference values distributed with the data set of Ref. [7, 17]. These values were computed with an exact sweeping-line solver, not with the qReduMIS pipeline [17]. Our transfer- matrix dynamic programming over the lattice columns, exact for these geometries since all atoms occupy integer lattice sites and the blockade couples only adjacent columns, reproduces both the optimum size and the exact ground-state degeneracy for all 121 reference instances that record them. Since the reference solver is also a sweep over the lattice, this agreement checks our implementation rather than constituting an independent certificate. It likewise reproduces every optimum quoted in this work, including all nine in  I and that of `L16\_seed4816` (64, with degeneracy 4480). We use these reference sizes both to identify which instances quantum hardware failed to solve and to quantify the residual gap of the post-processed solutions ( I). Reference optima are available for 39 of the 43 instances. For the four Benchmark instances, which carry no reference entry, we recomputed the optima directly on the<tbc>

<tbc>reconstructed unit-disk graphs, obtaining |MIS|=46, 47, 45, and 45 for `HP125`, `HP1412`, `HP1435`, and `HP1478`, respectively. Two exact methods with different structure, branch-and-bound with reduction rules and the transfer-matrix dynamic programming above, agree on all four. The latter also supplies their exact degeneracies, which are used for the Benchmark family in Section IIIE. Comparing against these references, the quantum seed pool sat strictly below the true optimum on 8 of the 43 instances: six of the nine hard instances (all but `L12\_seed2922`, `L14\_seed2480`, and `L15\_seed3591`, whose single best seed already sits at the optimum), the Benchmark instance `HP1435` (size 44 against a true optimum of 45, consistent with its reported QAA success rate of 0% [7]), and one standard instance, `L16\_seed4816` (size 63 against 64). On the remaining 35 instances the seed pool already reached the certified optimum, so the configurations discovered at that size are optimal as well. This does not make the pool as a whole optimal: it also retains smaller configurations.

## III. RESULTS

### A. Overview of Amplification Results

Figure 2 shows the amplification results for the 40 instances whose best independent-set size did not change under post-processing, grouped by type. The three instances where post-processing found a strictly larger independent set are treated separately in Section IIID. Across the full 43-instance dataset, Houdayer cluster updates consistently expand the quantum-generated solution pools: amplification factors range from \(1.0\times\) to \(11923\times\), with a median of \(24.3\times\) and a mean of \(657.2\times\). The distribution is strongly right-skewed, driven by a handful of instances with unusually large degenerate manifolds. Amplification was not universal, however: three instances with more than one distinct quantum solution showed none at all (`L3\_seed3849`, `L5\_seed4703`, and `L5\_seed2142`, all at exactly \(1.0\times\)). These are the smallest in the test bed, at 7, 20, and 20 atoms, and their seed pools already contained the complete ground-state manifold, so \(1.0\times\) is the best attainable result rather than a failure (Section IIIE).

Figure 3 shows the initial quantum solution counts against the final counts using Houdayer cluster updates. Most points lie above the diagonal, confirming amplification across all problem types and sizes. The four points on the diagonal are instances that showed no amplification. The spread along the vertical axis for fixed initial count illustrates that amplification is not simply proportional to the size of the quantum seed pool: instances with similar initial counts can differ by orders of magnitude in final count, reflecting differences in underlying manifold structure rather than sampling volume. Which of these two situations obtains is a property of the ground-state structure rather than of the pool size: Fig. 5<tbc>

<tbc>of Ref. \[19\] illustrates the distinction for two paradigmatic spin-glass instances, where a manifold made of many disconnected components in configuration space limits what any recombination move can reach, while a connected one does not.

The adaptive stopping criterion distributed efficiently across instances: 38 of 43 reached exhaustive pairwise exploration, while 5 saturated before processing all pairs, indicating early convergence on large manifolds. The maximum number of pairs processed in any pass was 16539, well below the 10<sup>5</sup> pair hard cutoff, confirming that the saturation heuristic reliably identifies manifold boundaries without wasting computation time. We stress that "exhaustive" here refers to processing every pair _within the given seed pool_. Such coverage still explores only the manifold region reachable from those seeds (Section IVC), and does not imply discovery of the complete ground-state manifold or of the global optimum.

## B. Amplification Patterns Across Problem Types

Amplification behavior differs systematically across the three instance families, reflecting distinct relationships between quantum seed quality and manifold structure.

## D. Classical Post-Processing Improves on Quantum Hardware for Hard Instances

For the nine hard instances we can compare our results directly against the exact reference optima of Section IIF. This comparison establishes two facts. First, quantum hardware failed to reach the true optimum on six of the nine hard instances, falling short by 1 to 4 atoms ( I), and on the other three it returned only a single solution at the optimum. ### F. Computational Efficiency

Figure 6 shows cluster-update time versus final solution count for the 40 instances whose size did not improve. All runs completed on a standard laptop [15], and the entire dataset, 2451 quantum seeds expanded to 2749146 validated configurations, required 1073 seconds of computation end to end, i.e., 18 minutes on a single laptop core. Almost all of it is the cluster-update loop: 870 seconds across the 43 first-level passes and 200 seconds for the higher-level passes of the three multilevel runs. The one-off repair of every post-selected hardware sample to a maximal independent set (Section IID) takes 2 seconds for all 18759 samples. Both stages are recovery costs. The post-hoc validation of Section IIF and the coverage certification of Section IIIE are analysis costs and are excluded. Of those configurations, 2485881 are certified optimal against the reference values. The remaining 263265, or 9.6%, belong to the 8 instances whose<tbc>

<tbc>seed pool sat below the certified optimum (Section IIF) and are validated at their best-found size rather than at the true optimum. The post-processing cost is small compared with the hardware time already expended: at a cycle time of about 0.1s [7], a 1000-shot run takes about 100s of device time per instance. Per family:

• **Benchmark instances**: from under 1 second (`HP125`, `HP1412`, with only 3 and 15 pairs) up to 580 seconds for instance `HP1478` (13530 pairs), spanning nearly four orders of magnitude in runtime.<tbc>

• **Hard instances**: from under 1 second up to 20 seconds (`L16\_seed4392`, 190 pairs), all reaching exhaustive pairwise exploration of their first- level seed pools. The two higher-level passes of `L17\_seed46` halted on saturation instead and took 200 seconds together.<tbc>

• **Standard instances**: from under 1 second to approximately 90 seconds, depending on manifold size.

Figure 6 plots cluster-update time rather than end-to- end time, because it is the exploration loop whose cost scales with the manifold being recovered. On that axis the log-log plot reveals a near-linear scaling of solution count with runtime, \(N_\mathrm{total}\propto t^{0.89}\) (_R_<sup>2</sup>=0.93), the exponent slightly below unity indicating modestly diminishing returns on additional computation. Substantial scatter remains about this trend: instances with comparable run times can differ by more than an order of magnitude in final count, because the per-pair cost (set by cluster count and repair complexity) varies by more than three orders of magnitude across the dataset, while the number of pairs required depends on seed-pool size.

The hard cutoff of 10<sup>5</sup> pair comparisons was never invoked, since the pass with the most pairs processed required only 16539. Combined with the modest hardware requirements, these results suggest Houdayer post- processing is a practical and lightweight component of any quantum optimization pipeline, as can also be seen in Fig. 6 where the scaling is close to linear.

## IV. DISCUSSION

### A. Why Houdayer Cluster Updates Work for the MIS Problem

The effectiveness of Houdayer cluster updates for MIS manifold exploration rests on a combination of structural and algorithmic properties that make it well-matched to the geometry of degenerate combinatorial optimization problems, especially for unit-disk quasi-two-dimensional graphs.

The key mechanism is nonlocal, rejection-free recombination. Local search moves such as single-vertex swaps [20] change one site at a time. Houdayer updates<tbc>

<tbc>instead identify entire connected components of disagreement between two solutions and swap them en bloc, enabling large-scale structural rearrangements in a single operation. Because the agreement backbone is preserved and every candidate is independent by construction (Section IIC), cluster exchanges are accepted with certainty. There is no energy barrier to overcome and no rejection step. To quantify the difference, we ran a local search from the same seed pools that moves a selected vertex to a free site with exactly one selected neighbor, keeping the set size, and whenever such a move frees a vertex adds it and continues from the larger set, with the same number of candidate evaluations as the cluster updates used on each instance. On the 30 instances with optimal seeds the two recover comparable numbers of configurations (local search more on 14, cluster updates more on 10, median ratio 1.00), but cluster updates recover more on 7 of the 8 largest manifolds, 1967339 against 911142 for `HP1478`, where one pair yields many configurations at once. From suboptimal seeds, the two methods improve the same three instances and neither improves the other five. Local search reaches the same sizes on `L12\_seed829` and `L17\_seed46` and one atom less on `L17\_seed424`, where it needs about \(3\times 10^4\) evaluations to reach the size-70 configurations that cluster updates find with 66 ( I). All configurations from both methods were validated as described in Section IIF.

For the MIS on unit disk graphs, the sparse and geometrically constrained edge structure causes the induced subgraph \(G[\Delta_{ij}]\) to break into several components, so a single pair generates 2_<sup>c</sup>_ candidates: over the 135202 seed pairs of the 30 instances with optimal seeds (at most 20000 per instance), the median is _c_=3 and the maximum _c_=13. The components are not restricted to the two-vertex form drawn in Figure 1: 57% contain one vertex from each parent and the remainder are larger, up to 44 vertices. The fan-out is unaffected by component size, since each component contributes one binary choice however many vertices it holds. Between maximum independent sets every component is balanced, and none of these pairs contains an imbalanced one. Between the suboptimal seeds of the other 7 instances with at least two of them, 0.16% of components are imbalanced, all but one of odd size, and these are the source of the size improvements in Section IIID. The exponential fan-out per pair is what drives the rapid manifold expansion observed across all instance types.

The complementarity with quantum sampling is also important. Quantum annealing explores the solution space through coherent tunneling and tends to cluster samples near local energy minima. Houdayer updates operate orthogonally: they systematically recombine structurally distinct solutions to reach regions of the ground- state manifold that neither single-solution perturbation nor further quantum sampling would easily access. The two methods are thus complementary. Quantum provides high-quality seeds, and classical cluster updates provide systematic coverage.

## B. Two Regimes: Amplification and Quality Improvement

Our results reveal two qualitatively distinct operating regimes for hybrid Houdayer cluster-update post- processing, determined by the relationship between quantum hardware capability and ground-state manifold structure.

In the **large manifold regime**, quantum hardware reaches the true ground state (verified against the reference optima, Section IIF) and produces an initial pool of diverse optimal solutions. Classical post-processing then systematically expands this pool by recombining seeds to reach structurally distant manifold regions. This regime dominates for the standard test bed and for those benchmark instances that combine a large degenerate manifold with a diverse seed pool, where amplification factors can reach 10<sup>3</sup>-10<sup>4</sup> times the original pool.

Amplification and solution quality are, however, largely decoupled, and the clearest illustration is instance `HP1435`. It is the hardest Benchmark instance (_H_=1435, QAA success rate 0% [7]), its quantum seeds sit one atom below the true optimum of 45, and Houdayer post-processing nonetheless amplified them \(1104\times\) into 118153 configurations, all at the suboptimal size 44. A large, diverse seed pool therefore guarantees a large final pool but says nothing about whether that pool sits at the optimum. Amplification quantity scales with the accessible manifold size and seed diversity rather than with hardness, and independently of whether the seeds are optimal: larger degenerate spaces offer more recombination opportunities, and high initial diversity (Figure 4) seeds broader exploration.

In the **difficult landscape regime**, quantum hardware does not reliably find the true ground state. The initial solution pool sits at a suboptimal energy level, and the Houdayer algorithm by operating on these seeds can construct recombinations that repair into higher-quality configurations. This regime characterizes the three hard instances where classical post-processing discovered strictly larger independent sets. Amplification in this regime is variable (from \(10\times\) for instance `L17\_seed424` up to \(1139\times\) for instance `L17\_seed46`). Both figures refer to the first-level pass, which expands the quantum seed pool at the seed size and is where the larger configurations are first discovered. The subsequent pass seeded by those configurations amplifies a different, smaller starting set, so ratios across the two levels are not comparable. The spread reflects how many configurations exist at the improved size, but the qualitative outcome, improvement in solution quality, is of greater practical interest than the raw count. It demonstrates that classical recombination can partially compensate for systematic biases in quantum sampling, and in one case close the gap to the true optimum.

Note that both regimes are not mutually exclusive, and this suggests a strategy we have not tested here. For the pure Houdayer update the combined energy of the<tbc>

<tbc>two-replica system is conserved, so pairing sub-optimal solutions should trade optimality between the two members of a pair: as one improves the other degrades, and retaining only the better member would drive a pool of sub-optimal solutions towards optimality. We note two caveats. The MIS repair step (Section IID) changes set sizes and therefore breaks the exact energy conservation the argument relies on, and no experiment in this work seeds the algorithm with a deliberately sub-optimal pool. We therefore offer this as a direction for future work rather than an established mechanism.

Classical post-processing thus provides a computationally cheap step that can partially mitigate poor quantum hardware performance.

### C. Limitations, Non-Ergodicity, and Future Directions

There are, however, limitations to cluster-update- based post-processing approaches. First, the Houdayer algorithm is fundamentally non-ergodic: it can only reach configurations obtainable by a single cluster exchange between two seeds. If the quantum seeds are all confined to a single pocket of the solution space, the algorithm will map only that disconnected pocket and leave other regions entirely unexplored. Coverage rises with the size of the seed pool and falls with the size of the manifold (Section IIIE). Increasing the number of quantum shots or diversifying the annealing schedule, for which systematic design methods now exist [21], would enlarge and diversify the seed pool and, in turn, improve manifold coverage. A further possibility for future work is to pool seeds from solvers with different sampling biases, for example quantum measurements together with a cheap classical heuristic, so that the sources populate complementary regions of the manifold. Alternatively, including less optimal solutions can allow the algorithm to climb over small barriers in the energy landscape by successively applying cluster updates. Second, we have not run the converse control of seeding the algorithm with cheap classical near-optima, either in place of the quantum seeds or mixed with them, so the marginal value of the quantum seeds specifically, as opposed to any sufficiently diverse near-optimal pool, is not isolated here. Ref. [11] addresses the bias-correction question for classical optimizers but not this comparison. Third, the approach is heuristic, i.e., there is no _a priori_ guarantee that all optima are found. Where a reference degeneracy is available this can be checked rather than assumed, and Section IIIE does so: coverage of the ground-state manifold ranges from 0.001% to 100%, and on six instances the recovered pool is provably complete. Completeness is therefore attainable, but only for manifolds small enough that a fixed seed budget can enumerate them. For applications that require solution diversity rather than completeness, a finite number of uncorrelated solutions is often sufficient. Fourth, the exploration scales as O(|S<sub>0</sub>|<sup>2</sup>)<tbc>

<tbc>in the size of the _seed_ pool, which becomes costly for very large seed sets. However, our saturation-based stopping criterion mitigates this in practice. Finally, all instances in this study are unit disk graphs arising from Rydberg atom array geometries. The effectiveness of Houdayer updates on graphs where clusters percolate (e.g., power- law distribution of nodes as in scale-free graphs or higher dimensions) degrades rapidly. However, some improvement might be achievable even in these cases for sections of the ground-state manifold.

Houdayer cluster updates are not specific to MIS. The core mechanism of symmetric difference decomposition into independent clusters, rejection-free exchange applies to any combinatorial problem where solutions can be represented as binary assignments and pairs of solutions generate a well-defined overlap structure. It carries over without a new repair step to maximum clique and minimum vertex cover, through their equivalence to the MIS problem, and to weighted MIS, where the exchange still preserves independence and changes the weight by the difference between the two sides of each cluster. Other candidates, such as constraint satisfaction problems with degenerate solution spaces, would need a repair step adapted to their feasibility structure.

## V. CONCLUSION

We have measured how much ground-state information a neutral atom MIS measurement record contains beyond the solutions the device reports. Across 43 instances from QuEra’s Aquila Rydberg device, classical post-processing via Houdayer cluster updates recovers between 1.0\(\times\) and 11923\(\times\) as many distinct configurations at the certified-or-best-found size (median 24.3\(\times\), and 8.9\(\times\) over the 35 instances whose seeds were already optimal), turning pools of tens to hundreds of configurations into collections with a median of 463 and as many as nearly two million. The entire dataset required 18 minutes of computation on a single laptop core, measured end to end, compared with about 100s of device time for each 1000-shot hardware run.

Two features of this data set make the measurement possible. First, exact ground-state degeneracies are available for these instances, so the recovered fraction is a number rather than a bound: a median of 21% of the true manifold, and on six instances provably all of it. The non- ergodicity of the method is thus quantified rather than disclaimed, and its practical boundary identified, namely that completeness is reachable when the manifold is small enough for a fixed seed budget to enumerate, and that coverage falls steeply as the manifold grows. Second, the same exact references reveal that the quantum seed pool sat below the true optimum on 8 of the 43 instances. Amplification and solution quality are therefore separate axes: a run can be amplified a thousandfold and still describe a suboptimal manifold, and only an exact reference distinguishes the two cases.

<tbc>For three hard instances, classical post-processing discovered independent sets strictly larger than any in the seed pool, and on one of them, `L12\_seed829`, it reached the certified optimum and recovered its entire 18-configuration manifold. All 15511 improved solutions passed independence, maximality, and target-cardinality validation. Because a local search from the same seeds reaches the same sizes on two of the three, the improvements show what recombination can extract from near- optimal seeds rather than an advantage specific to cluster updates.

The practical consequence is that solution counts and diversity metrics reported directly from quantum hardware understand what a run has determined, by a median factor of 14 on this dataset and by up to four orders of magnitude in the extreme case. For any application whose figure of merit is the number or diversity of optimal configurations rather than a single best solution, the quantity worth reporting is the post-processed count, since the recovery costs seconds to minutes of laptop time per instance. Because the cluster exchange mechanism is not specific to MIS, the same measurement can be made for any problem whose solutions admit a binary encoding and a well-defined overlap structure, which is where we expect this accounting to matter next.
